newsitem.title: TURKEY: FEATURE - Turks see troubled economy but no crisis in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Turks see troubled economy but no crisis in 1997.

text.p: After a troubled year, the Turkish economy is expected to suffer more economic pain in 1997 but no severe crisis unless political instability returns to mar the outlook, economic analysts say.

The economy was under pressure in 1996 from chronic inflation of about 80 percent and big public deficits, expected to reach more than 10 percent of gross domestic product. At the same time, Turkey faced fresh political turmoil and uncertainty.
Gross national product is likely to rise by some seven percent and current accounts may yield a deficit of about $6.9 billion, analysts said.
"There is no possibility of a crisis in 1997, but it will be a tough year," said Esfender Korkmaz, head of the economics faculty at Istanbul University.
Korkmaz estimated 1997 year-on-year inflation at around 85 to 90 percent and a current account deficit at $6 billion.
IMF TALKS COULD PRODUCE NEW PROGRAMME
The key to the course of 1997 economic policies will be the outcome of talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), expected to resume in late January or early February.

"Right now it is hard to say whether we will reach a stand-by accord or a long-term accord. But I can say that the government is politically positive towards a deal with the IMF," Treasury chief Mehmet Kaytaz told Reuters.
Economists said Turkey, which disclosed its 1997 economic targets in October, might need to draw up a new economic plan under IMF guidance to win the support of the Fund.

The IMF would probably urge Turkey to take structural measures to curb inflation and narrow fiscal deficits, widened also by huge military spending to try to quell a Kurdish guerrilla uprising in the southeast of the country.
Kaytaz said structural measures are also needed to reduce high interest rates.
"For a permanent decline in domestic interest rates, Turkey should increase tax revenues, reform the pension system and speed up privatisation," Kaytaz said.
The cash-short treasury now offers high real returns of up to 40 percent to borrow from the domestic market as part of its effort to finance fiscal deficits.
A high borrowing requirement for the treasury pushes up domestic rates and leaves less money for the private sector to expand business.
BORROWING COSTS COULD RISE
Turkish officials said the government should rely more on foreign funding sources to relieve the burden of costly domestic borrowing.
"Foreign borrowing will not be very different next year. The borrowing volume might stand at around this year's level," Kaytaz said.
After Standard & Poor downgraded Turkey's long-term debt rating to B from B+ this month, some bankers fear Moody's may follow the move by cutting Turkey's Ba3 rating in early 1997.
"Turkey's foreign borrowing will be more expensive. But it may offset the effect of credit downgradings by reaching a deal with the IMF," said a senior private banker.
Kaytaz said any accord with the IMF would ease Turkey's borrowing in international markets. "But it will have a very marginal effect on our borrowing if we cannot reach a deal," he said.
QUICK PRIVATISATION
Turkish brokers and businessmen said the government should accelerate the stagnant sell-off programme, which raised some $3 billion in the past decade -- against a goal of $2 billion for 1996 alone.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, who has been a leading opponent of privatisation during the past five years, has now pledged to speed sell-offs in a radical U-turn. But opposition MPs are preparing to block his efforts in the courts.

Erbakan's government is planning to privatise parts of the Tupras refining company, petroleum distributor Petrol Ofisi the iron and steel maker Eregli, the petrochemicals company Petkim And Turk Telekom in 1997.
"The markets may enter into a mood of optimism if Turkey can succeed at privatisation of at least several of them," said Alp Tekince, assistant general manager of Bumerang Securities.
POLITICAL CRISIS COULD CHANGE SCENARIO
The 1997 economic scenario, drawn up by the government and market players, could change drastically if Turkey falls into a fresh political crisis.

Erbakan's Islamist-centre right coalition government holds a narrow majority in parliament. But increasing pressure from the opposition might drag the country towards early elections or months of searching for a new government, analysts said.
That would delay desperately needed action to rescue the economy, as happened in the first half of 1996.
Bankers said any new political crisis might doom the present financial stability, secured partly by the central bank's tight grip on the market.
